name: sample/power/data/power_system.yaml
text:
# The power sample's power system: the solar panels, the battery and the power
# conditioning. The panels are the cells on the four wing panels, which turn to
# the sun, and the cells on the deck, which do not.
#
# The power generation notebook reads the panels, with scenario.yaml from this
# folder. The power budget notebook reads the whole file, with the consumption
# file too. Edit this file and run the notebooks again. They never write it.
#
# The power of a panel is the solar flux x its area x fill_ratio x
# cell_efficiency x loss_factor x the cosine of the sun's angle to the cells. It
# is scaled by the light that the Earth does not hide, and by the share of the
# panel that the rest of the model does not shade.

# The cells' efficiency at their rated temperature, such as triple-junction GaAs
# cells at about 30%.
cell_efficiency: 30 %

# Every loss up to the array's output, as the share of the power left: the cells'
# temperature, ageing, mismatch between cells, UV, and the array's own wiring.
# Set it for the year being sized, such as the end of life. 0.80 keeps 80%: about
# 0.92 for cells some 40 C above their rated temperature, 0.93 for 7 years of
# ageing, and 0.95 for the rest. The conditioning below takes the power on from
# the array's output.
loss_factor: 0.80

# The panels, each under a name of your choice. A panel names its part in the
# 3D model, which gives its area and the direction its cells face. The part must
# be flat, as a face of cells is. A part on a wing turns with the wing's
# articulation in scenario.yaml. fill_ratio is the share of the part that the
# cells cover.
panels:
  wing +y inner: {part: Wing +y inner cells, fill_ratio: 85 %}
  wing +y outer: {part: Wing +y outer cells, fill_ratio: 85 %}
  wing -y inner: {part: Wing -y inner cells, fill_ratio: 85 %}
  wing -y outer: {part: Wing -y outer cells, fill_ratio: 85 %}
  deck: {part: Deck cells, fill_ratio: 80 %}
  # Or a panel typed in, with the direction its cells face in body axes and its
  # area, for a model with no panels, or none at all. It stays fixed in body axes,
  # is never shaded, and shades nothing. The notebook notes each one.
  # side +x: {normal: +x, area: 0.2 m2, fill_ratio: 80 %}
  # tilted: {normal: [0, 1, -1], area: 0.1 m2, fill_ratio: 80 %}

# Whether the rest of the model shades the panels, such as the payload housing
# shading the deck cells. points is about how many sample points each panel
# gets: more give a finer lit fraction, and take longer. Leave the block out, or
# set enabled: false, for no shading.
self_shadowing: {enabled: true, points: 512}

# The battery. capacity is what it holds when new and full: here Saft VES16
# cells, 8 in series and 8 strings in parallel, 64 cells of 4.5 A h and 16 W h.
# capacity_factor is the share left in the year being sized, after fade.
# max_depth_of_discharge is the deepest it may go in each orbit: 30% is a usual
# limit in low orbit, where it cycles some 5500 times a year. initial_charge is
# the charge at the start of the run, 100% if left out.
battery:
  capacity: 1024 W h
  capacity_factor: 0.80
  max_depth_of_discharge: 30 %
  initial_charge: 100 %

# The power conditioning: an efficiency for each path the energy takes. From the
# array to the bus through the array regulator; from the bus into the battery
# through the charge regulator and the cells; back out through the discharge
# regulator and the cells; and from the bus to the loads through the switches and
# the harness. Energy that goes through the battery pays both of its paths.
conditioning:
  array_regulator: 0.96
  battery_charge: 0.95
  battery_discharge: 0.95
  distribution: 0.97

# The margin on all the loads together, on top of each equipment's margin in the
# consumption file. 5% suits a mature design.
system_margin: 5 %

name: sample/power/data/scenario.yaml
text:
# The power sample's scenario: three orbits of a 510 km sun-synchronous orbit.
#
# A copy of the scenario sample, sample/scenario/data/scenario.yaml, with the
# power sample's 3D model. Power keeps its own copies of the scenario files, so
# that this folder stands on its own, and one power setup can be checked against
# several scenarios. The power generation notebook reads this file, and never
# writes it.

orbit:
  # The orbit is given one of four ways. Here, a sun-synchronous orbit, for which
  # quicksat builds the TLE, with its epoch at the start time below. The altitude
  # is averaged over one orbit. Give the local time of the ascending node, ltan,
  # or of the descending node, ltdn, 12 h away: ltdn: "01:30" is the same orbit.
  # Write the time in quotes: YAML reads an unquoted 13:30 as the number 810.
  sso: {altitude: 510 km, ltan: "13:30"}
  # Or a TLE file with exactly one TLE. A relative path is taken from the folder
  # of this file. This one is a 510 km orbit at 10:30 LTAN, with its epoch at the
  # start time below.
  # tle_file: sso_510km.tle
  # Or an OMM file with exactly one element set, in KVN, XML, JSON or CSV.
  # omm_file: my_satellite.omm
  # Or a trajectory file with positions and velocities at times: ECSV, or a
  # CCSDS OEM in KVN. See docs/scenario/scenario_ref.ipynb for the layouts.
  # trajectory_file: my_orbit.oem

# UTC. YAML turns an unquoted ISO time into a datetime, and that is accepted.
start: 2026-10-01T09:00:00
duration: 3 orbits
# The orbit and the eclipses are evaluated on this grid. The default is 10 s.
step: 10 s

# The spacecraft's 3D model: a GLB file in body axes and metres, with its origin
# at the point the body turns about. A relative path is taken from the folder of
# this file. Power takes the panels from its parts: the cells on the four wing
# panels, which turn, and the cells on the deck, around the payload housing,
# which do not. The rest of the model can shade them.
3d_model:
  file: spacecraft.glb
  # The parts of the model that turn to face the sun. Each wing is one node of the
  # model, with its origin on the wing's drive axis. The wing turns about y until
  # its cells, which face -z as the model draws them, point as close to the sun as
  # they can. In imaging, the wings park at 0 deg instead, as the model draws them.
  # An optional range, such as range: [-90 deg, 90 deg], limits the turn.
  # point gives that axis and its direction: the sun here, or any direction an
  # attitude can use, such as a ground target for an antenna.
  articulations:
    wing +y: {part: Wing +y, axis: +y, point: [-z, sun], park: {imaging: 0 deg}}
    wing -y: {part: Wing -y, axis: +y, point: [-z, sun], park: {imaging: 0 deg}}

# Ground points that an attitude can point at, by any name. Optional. Here, the
# SvalSat ground station on Svalbard, which the downlink tracks. The altitude is
# above the WGS84 ellipsoid, and 0 m if left out. The triggers Svalbard rise and
# Svalbard set find when it sees the satellite above min_elevation, 5 deg if left
# out.
gnd_targets:
  Svalbard: {latitude: 78.229 deg, longitude: 15.408 deg, altitude: 500 m}

# The attitudes, each under a name of your choice, which the activities use. An
# attitude fixes one body axis on a direction (point), and turns a second body
# axis as close as it can get to another direction (constrain). The directions
# are nadir, sun, orbit normal, velocity, ground velocity, and the names in
# gnd_targets.
attitudes:
  # +z points at the Earth and -y runs along the orbit normal. The body axes then
  # match LVLH: x along the track, y minus the orbit normal and z nadir.
  nadir: {point: [+z, nadir], constrain: [-y, orbit normal]}
  # -z points at the sun. The -y axis stays along the orbit normal, so the body
  # stays still over an orbit. Constraining an axis to nadir instead keeps it
  # facing the Earth, but the body spins fast when the sun is close to the nadir
  # line. Where the sun lies along the orbit normal, nadir takes its place.
  sun pointing: {point: [-z, sun], constrain: [-y, orbit normal]}
  # For imaging: +z at nadir, and x along the ground's motion below the satellite,
  # so that the detector's lines stay across it. This is nadir turned in yaw by up
  # to about 4 degrees, most at the equator.
  yaw steering: {point: [+z, nadir], constrain: [+x, ground velocity]}
  # For the downlink: +z, where the antenna is, tracks the ground station.
  track Svalbard: {point: [+z, Svalbard], constrain: [-y, orbit normal]}
  # Another example, not used by the activities below: a 30 deg roll off nadir,
  # a turn about x after the nadir orientation.
  # roll 30: {point: [+z, nadir], constrain: [-y, orbit normal], offset: [x 30 deg]}

# How the body turns from one attitude to another. Before each activity whose
# attitude differs from the one before, the body turns from rest to rest about one
# axis, then settles. The turn takes the end of the activity before, so each
# activity starts in its own attitude. Its time grows with the angle. These values
# are close to the sizing sample's agility budget, but nothing reads them from it.
# Leave the block out for instant changes.
slew:
  # The fastest the body turns.
  max_rate: 0.7 deg/s
  # How fast the turn speeds up and slows down.
  max_acceleration: 0.08 deg/s2
  # The time to settle after the turn.
  settling_time: 20 s

# One repeat of the list. The run repeats it until the duration ends, and cuts
# the last activity there. Each activity is a chain link: it starts where the one
# before it ends. The fields are
#   the title: any text that names what the activity is for, such as imaging
#     45 deg lat. The tables, the Gantt chart, the warnings and the viewer use it
#   the trigger that ends it: a duration such as 20 min, or the next event after
#     the activity starts. The events are the shadow edges, eclipse entry, umbra
#     entry, umbra exit and eclipse exit; ascending node and descending node; and
#     latitude crossings such as latitude 30 deg ascending, latitude -30 deg
#     descending, or latitude 45 deg for either direction; and a target's rise
#     and set, such as Svalbard rise. An event can take an offset, such as
#     eclipse entry + 2 min
#   the attitude: one of the names under attitudes
#   the mode: any name but slew, which the run gives the mode while the body
#     turns
#   the constraint, optional: the illumination it expects. sunlit, penumbra,
#     umbra, or eclipse for either of the last two
#
# Each orbit: idle in sun pointing, imaging around the 45 deg crossing going north,
# the Svalbard pass near the northern turn, then nadir through the eclipse. The
# imaging ends 5 min after the crossing, because the turn to Svalbard takes about
# 1.6 min of it: the imaging holds about 5 min, above the 4% of the orbit it needs.
# Svalbard rises within a minute or so of that. The downlink ends 2 min after
# Svalbard sets, because the turn to nadir takes about 2 min of it, so the antenna
# stays on the station until it sets. The pass ends a few minutes before the
# eclipse. Neither gap leaves time to turn to sun pointing and back.
activities:
  - [power generation, latitude 45 deg -2 min, sun pointing, idle, sunlit]
  - [imaging 45 deg lat, latitude 45 deg +5 min, yaw steering, imaging, sunlit]
  - [downlink Svalbard, Svalbard set + 2 min, track Svalbard, downlink]
  - [nadir before eclipse, eclipse entry, nadir, idle, sunlit]
  - [eclipse in nadir, eclipse exit, nadir, idle, eclipse]

  - [imaging 45 deg lat, latitude 45 deg +5 min, yaw steering, imaging, sunlit]
  - [downlink Svalbard, Svalbard set + 2 min, track Svalbard, downlink]

# Attitude agility settings: the spacecraft cases that can be slewed, the wheels
# that slew them, and how long the platform takes to settle afterwards.
#
# No mass anywhere. The mass budget owns it, and a second copy here would drift --
# the same reason altitude lives only in mission.yaml. Orbit comes from mission.yaml,
# for ground track speed. The target duration for a manoeuvre is not here
# either: that is asked of a spacecraft, not a property of one. It is in
# requirements.yaml.

# The inertia case that the budget sizes and checks. The others are kept for
# comparison, such as the spacecraft at other stages of the mission.
selected_case: first_guess

inertia_cases:
  # One case is one spacecraft, one set of mass properties. The names are yours
  # -- nothing in the code matches on them. Each case is EITHER an envelope
  # estimate OR a stated inertia, never both, so there is never a question which
  # of the two produced a number.

  # Inertia estimated from a uniform box.
  first_guess:
    # The box: x along track, y cross track, z nadir.
    body:
      x: 1.5 m
      y: 1.5 m
      z: 2.0 m
    # Uplift for arrays, radiator and booms. It is per axis, because the
    # appendages are not symmetric.
    appendage_factor:
      roll: 1.07
      pitch: 1.02
    # Of the load still aboard. The mass comes from the mass budget and this
    # picks the mission point, so the inertia follows the mass automatically.
    propellant: 100 %

  # Stated outright, as a mass properties report gives it. NOTE: a stated
  # inertia is a fixed number. It does not follow the mass budget, and nothing
  # checks that it still describes the spacecraft you costed.
  measured_bol:
    inertia:
      roll: 264.7 kg*m**2
      pitch: 280.0 kg*m**2

  # The same spacecraft, tanks empty.
  measured_eol:
    inertia:
      roll: 250.0 kg*m**2
      pitch: 264.0 kg*m**2

# A pyramid, with its symmetry axis along yaw. The momentum and the torque are
# nameplate figures, per wheel. The use factor and the derating are policy: the
# rest of the momentum is disturbance storage, and the rest of the torque is
# control authority.
wheels:
  count: 4
  # Of each wheel above the pyramid base plane.
  elevation: 26.5 deg
  momentum: 4.0 N*m*s
  torque: 0.2 N*m
  momentum_use_factor: 33.3 %
  torque_derating: 75 %

# What the platform needs after a slew before the payload can work. An ADCS
# property, applied once at the end of a manoeuvre and not between steps.
settling_time: 20 s

name: docs/power/data/power_system.yaml
text:
# The reference power system of docs/power/: the solar panels, the battery and the
# power conditioning. The panels are the cells on the four wing panels, which
# turn to the sun, and the cells on the deck, which do not.
#
# A copy of the power sample's file. The reference notebooks quote figures from
# it, so it changes only together with them. They never write it.
#
# The power of a panel is the solar flux x its area x fill_ratio x
# cell_efficiency x loss_factor x the cosine of the sun's angle to the cells. It
# is scaled by the light that the Earth does not hide, and by the share of the
# panel that the rest of the model does not shade.

# The cells' efficiency at their rated temperature, such as triple-junction GaAs
# cells at about 30%.
cell_efficiency: 30 %

# Every loss up to the array's output, as the share of the power left: the cells'
# temperature, ageing, mismatch between cells, UV, and the array's own wiring.
# Set it for the year being sized, such as the end of life. 0.80 keeps 80%: about
# 0.92 for cells some 40 C above their rated temperature, 0.93 for 7 years of
# ageing, and 0.95 for the rest. The conditioning below takes the power on from
# the array's output.
loss_factor: 0.80

# The panels, each under a name of your choice. A panel names its part in the
# 3D model, which gives its area and the direction its cells face. The part must
# be flat, as a face of cells is. A part on a wing turns with the wing's
# articulation in scenario.yaml. fill_ratio is the share of the part that the
# cells cover.
panels:
  wing +y inner: {part: Wing +y inner cells, fill_ratio: 85 %}
  wing +y outer: {part: Wing +y outer cells, fill_ratio: 85 %}
  wing -y inner: {part: Wing -y inner cells, fill_ratio: 85 %}
  wing -y outer: {part: Wing -y outer cells, fill_ratio: 85 %}
  deck: {part: Deck cells, fill_ratio: 80 %}
  # Or a panel typed in, with the direction its cells face in body axes and its
  # area, for a model with no panels, or none at all. It stays fixed in body axes,
  # is never shaded, and shades nothing. The notebook notes each one.
  # side +x: {normal: +x, area: 0.2 m2, fill_ratio: 80 %}
  # tilted: {normal: [0, 1, -1], area: 0.1 m2, fill_ratio: 80 %}

# Whether the rest of the model shades the panels, such as the payload housing
# shading the deck cells. points is about how many sample points each panel
# gets: more give a finer lit fraction, and take longer. Leave the block out, or
# set enabled: false, for no shading.
self_shadowing: {enabled: true, points: 512}

# The battery. capacity is what it holds when new and full: here Saft VES16
# cells, 8 in series and 8 strings in parallel, 64 cells of 4.5 A h and 16 W h.
# capacity_factor is the share left in the year being sized, after fade.
# max_depth_of_discharge is the deepest it may go in each orbit: 30% is a usual
# limit in low orbit, where it cycles some 5500 times a year. initial_charge is
# the charge at the start of the run, 100% if left out.
battery:
  capacity: 1024 W h
  capacity_factor: 0.80
  max_depth_of_discharge: 30 %
  initial_charge: 100 %

# The power conditioning: an efficiency for each path the energy takes. From the
# array to the bus through the array regulator; from the bus into the battery
# through the charge regulator and the cells; back out through the discharge
# regulator and the cells; and from the bus to the loads through the switches and
# the harness. Energy that goes through the battery pays both of its paths.
conditioning:
  array_regulator: 0.96
  battery_charge: 0.95
  battery_discharge: 0.95
  distribution: 0.97

# The margin on all the loads together, on top of each equipment's margin in the
# consumption file. 5% suits a mature design.
system_margin: 5 %

attitudes:

  # match LVLH: x along the track, y minus the orbit normal and z nadir.
  nadir: {point: [+z, nadir], constrain: [-y, orbit normal]}

  # stays still over an orbit. Constraining an axis to nadir instead keeps it
  # facing the Earth, but the body spins fast when the sun is close to the nadir
  # line. Where the sun lies along the orbit normal, nadir takes its place.
  sun pointing: {point: [-z, sun], constrain: [-y, orbit normal]}

  # so that the detector's lines stay across it. This is nadir turned in yaw by up
  # to about 4 degrees, most at the equator.
  yaw steering: {point: [+z, nadir], constrain: [+x, ground velocity]}
  # For the downlink: +z, where the antenna is, tracks the ground station.
  track Svalbard: {point: [+z, Svalbard], constrain: [-y, orbit normal]}

  # a turn about x after the nadir orientation.
  # roll 30: {point: [+z, nadir], constrain: [-y, orbit normal], offset: [x 30 deg]}

# attitude differs from the one before, the body turns from rest to rest about one
# axis, then settles. The turn takes the end of the activity before, so each
# activity starts in its own attitude. Its time grows with the angle. These values
# are close to the sizing sample's agility budget, but nothing reads them from it.
# Leave the block out for instant changes.
slew:

  max_rate: 0.7 deg/s
  # How fast the turn speeds up and slows down.
  max_acceleration: 0.08 deg/s2
  # The time to settle after the turn.
  settling_time: 20 s

# the last activity there. Each activity is a chain link: it starts where the one
# before it ends. The fields are
#   the title: any text that names what the activity is for, such as imaging
#     45 deg lat. The tables, the Gantt chart, the warnings and the viewer use it
#   the trigger that ends it: a duration such as 20 min, or the next event after
#     the activity starts. The events are the shadow edges, eclipse entry, umbra
#     entry, umbra exit and eclipse exit; ascending node and descending node; and
#     latitude crossings such as latitude 30 deg ascending, latitude -30 deg
#     descending, or latitude 45 deg for either direction; and a target's rise
#     and set, such as Svalbard rise. An event can take an offset, such as
#     eclipse entry + 2 min
#   the attitude: one of the names under attitudes
#   the mode: any name but slew, which the run gives the mode while the body
#     turns
#   the constraint, optional: the illumination it expects. sunlit, penumbra,
#     umbra, or eclipse for either of the last two
#
# Each orbit: idle in sun pointing, imaging around the 45 deg crossing going north,
# the Svalbard pass near the northern turn, then nadir through the eclipse. The
# imaging ends 5 min after the crossing, because the turn to Svalbard takes about
# 1.6 min of it: the imaging holds about 5 min, above the 4% of the orbit it needs.
# Svalbard rises within a minute or so of that. The downlink ends 2 min after
# Svalbard sets, because the turn to nadir takes about 2 min of it, so the antenna
# stays on the station until it sets. The pass ends a few minutes before the
# eclipse. Neither gap leaves time to turn to sun pointing and back.
activities:
  - [power generation, latitude 45 deg -2 min, sun pointing, idle, sunlit]
  - [imaging 45 deg lat, latitude 45 deg +5 min, yaw steering, imaging, sunlit]
  - [downlink Svalbard, Svalbard set + 2 min, track Svalbard, downlink]
  - [nadir before eclipse, eclipse entry, nadir, idle, sunlit]
  - [eclipse in nadir, eclipse exit, nadir, idle, eclipse]
